summary: Proposes experimental TLS extensions that use opaque pinning tickets to pin a server's identity. In the first session the server gives the client an encrypted ticket, and on later connections the server proves it still holds the matching secret, which helps spot a wrongly issued certificate.

eli5.summary: The first time you meet, the server hands you a secret token. Next time, only the real server can show it knows what the token means, so impostors are caught.

questions: how to pin tls server identity
what is tls server identity pinning
how to detect misissued tls certificate
subtitle: TLS extensions that automatically detect when a server changes, using an encrypted secret shared on the first connection.

tldr.problem: A certificate authority might issue a certificate for a domain to an attacker, and a TLS client cannot easily detect this. Once the client has connected to the correct server once, it would be useful to ensure that future connections go to the same server, not an attacker with a fake certificate.
tldr.mechanism: On an initial TLS connection, the server generates an encrypted ticket containing a pinning secret derived from the key exchange. On subsequent connections, the client sends the ticket and the server proves it can decrypt it, proving it holds the corresponding secret. The proof is bound to the server's current public key, so an attacker cannot replay it.
tldr.outcome: This experimental RFC proposes a second factor for server authentication. It is a trust-on-first-use protocol: if the first connection is legitimate, all future connections are protected for the lifetime of the ticket.

today: RFC 8672 is Experimental. The authors plan to propose it as a Proposed Standard after two years of deployment experience. No standardization path is guaranteed.

sections.title: Server Identity and Trust-on-First-Use
sections.content:
A TLS client normally authenticates a server using a certificate chain rooted in a trusted certificate authority (CA). However, a CA might be compromised or coerced into issuing a certificate for the wrong domain. This RFC proposes an additional layer of server authentication: server identity pinning using opaque tickets.

The solution is based on trust-on-first-use (TOFU): the first time a client connects to a server and authenticates normally, it receives an encrypted pinning ticket. The client keeps this ticket. On later connections, it proves the server still possesses the corresponding secret, confirming that it is the same server. The approach does not require the client to explicitly manage pins or the administrator to configure anything beyond a ticket lifetime.
sections.eli5: The first time you talk to someone, you exchange a secret. Next time, they prove they still have that secret, so you know it is really them.

sections.title: How Pinning Tickets Work
sections.content:
During the TLS 1.3 handshake, after the server and client agree on a shared secret from the key exchange, the server generates a pinning secret from that handshake secret using a key derivation function. The server encrypts this secret into an opaque pinning ticket and sends it to the client in an EncryptedExtensions message. The client only accepts the ticket after verifying the server's certificate in the normal way.

The client caches the ticket and on the next connection to the same server (identified by hostname, protocol, and port), it sends the ticket as part of a PinningTicket extension in the ClientHello. The server decrypts the ticket, extracts the pinning secret, and computes a proof using the HMAC of that secret combined with the current session and the server's public key. The client verifies this proof and confirms that the server is legitimate.

On each successful connection, the server returns a fresh ticket with a new lifetime, so tokens are not fixed identifiers.
sections.eli5: Step one: the server hands you an encrypted token. Step two: next time, you hand it back and the server proves they can unlock it. If they can, it is the real server.

sections.title: Operational Requirements and Key Management
sections.content:
The main operational requirement is that if a server is part of a cluster, the pinning protection keys (used to encrypt tickets) must be synchronized between all cluster members. The RFC recommends deriving these keys from existing session resumption keys if those are already synchronized, minimizing additional work.

Server administrators set a ticket lifetime (typically 7 to 31 days), which is a commitment to retain the key for that duration. Keys should be rotated before expiry. If a key is compromised, it must be rotated, but the server continues accepting old tickets for a grace period to avoid locking out clients.

Unlike certificate pinning, server identity pinning does not break when the server renews its certificate or changes its public key. The server identity is tied to the pinning protection key, not the certificate or public key.
sections.eli5: All servers in a cluster must know the secret. Administrators pick how long to keep the secret safe. When the secret is revealed, it is replaced, but the old secret still works for a while so people do not get locked out.

sections.title: Security Properties and Limitations
sections.content:
This protocol is a second factor and does not weaken normal TLS authentication. It only activates after the certificate is verified. If a certificate is revoked, the client must refuse the connection regardless of any pinning behavior.

The pinning proof includes a hash of the server's public key to prevent an active attacker with real-time access to the original server from forging a valid proof. However, the protocol is vulnerable to initial MITM attacks: if an attacker intercepts the first connection, the client will pin to the attacker's identity and subsequent legitimate connections will fail. Clients should be given a way to remove corrupted pins.

The protocol does not protect against pervasive monitoring (always-active proxies that intercept all traffic). However, to reduce privacy concerns, the server should issue a fresh ticket on each connection so that a static ticket does not serve as a fixed client identifier.
sections.eli5: This adds a second lock on the door, but someone who tricks you the first time is not caught. If your secret is exposed, anyone can fake being the server, but you know something is wrong.

sections.title: Scope, Limitations and Future Standardization
sections.content:
This extension applies only to TLS 1.3. Earlier versions do not provide the encrypted handshake extension mechanism needed to transport the ticket securely. The protocol is not used with Pre-Shared Key (PSK) handshakes, only with certificate-based key exchanges, since it is designed to detect misissued certificates.

The document is Experimental and describes the goals for the experiment: confirm that non-supporting clients and servers are unaffected, that supporting clients and servers maintain connectivity, that enterprise middleboxes do not interfere, and that misissued certificates and rogue proxies are detected. Following two years of successful deployment, the authors plan to submit the protocol as a Proposed Standard.
sections.eli5: This only works with the newest TLS version. It is a test to see if the idea works well in the real world before making it official.
